title: Infosys Dividend 2026: Understanding Your Payout and Returns
description: Infosys announced an interim dividend of ₹26 per equity share for FY27 on October 23. The record date for this interim dividend is set for tomorrow, November .

faq.a: An interim dividend is a dividend paid by a company to its shareholders during the course of a financial year, before the final annual results are declared and the annual general meeting is held. It's usually based on the company's performance in the initial quarters.

faq.q: How is the record date different from the ex-dividend date?
faq.a: The record date is the cut-off date by which you must be listed as a shareholder to receive the dividend. The ex-dividend date is typically one business day before the record date. If you buy shares on or after the ex-dividend date, you will not be entitled to the upcoming dividend payment.

faq.q: How are Infosys dividends taxed for resident Indians?
faq.a: For resident Indians, dividend income is added to your total income and taxed at your applicable income tax slab rates. There is no Dividend Distribution Tax (DDT) paid by the company anymore, and the entire dividend amount is taxable in the recipient's hands.

faq.q: Do NRIs pay tax on Infosys dividends?
faq.a: Yes, NRIs are also subject to tax on dividend income in India. Generally, TDS (Tax Deducted at Source) is applied by the company at a rate of 20%, though this can be lower based on applicable Double Taxation Avoidance Agreements (DTAA) between India and the NRI's country of residence.

faq.q: What is dividend yield, and why is it important?
faq.a: Dividend yield is a financial ratio that shows how much a company pays out in dividends each year relative to its stock price. It's calculated as annual dividend per share divided by the share price. It's important for income-focused investors as it indicates the return on investment purely from dividends.

faq.q: Can I reinvest my Infosys dividend automatically?
faq.a: While some companies offer Dividend Reinvestment Plans (DRIPs), most Indian companies credit the dividend directly to your bank account. You would then need to manually use these funds to purchase more shares if you wish to reinvest.
